title: The Son of David, Born of Mary
sum: Matthew begins with a family history. In three sets of fourteen generations it runs from Abraham, through King David, through the disaster of the exile to Babylon, to Jesus, "the one called the Messiah." Four surprising women break the line of men: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Uriah's wife. Then the pattern breaks at the end: Joseph does not father Jesus. Mary is pregnant from the Holy Spirit before her marriage is complete.

Joseph, a righteous man, plans to end the marriage quietly, but an angel in a dream tells him to take Mary home and to name the child Jesus, "for he is the one who will save his people from their sins." Matthew sees in this the first of many fulfillments of Scripture: the virgin's son named Immanuel, "God is with us." Joseph obeys, and by naming the boy he makes him a son of David.
readings: Matthew drew on Israel's records (Ruth 4; 1 Chronicles 1–3) and on family tradition, and he reports what Joseph's family believed about Jesus' birth. Luke independently tells of the same virginal conception, Joseph of David's line, and the birth in Bethlehem, so both Gospels rest on a tradition older than either. The list is real history shaped to show a pattern.
Read as theology in story form

Matthew writes a carefully built prologue that answers who Jesus is (son of David, son of Abraham, Immanuel) and where he comes from (from the Holy Spirit). The counted generations, the women, the dream and the Scripture quotation are theology told as a story, and the reader is meant to see God steering Israel's history to its goal.

views.H: Royal family lists were treasured in Jesus' time, and Julius Africanus (in Eusebius, Church History 1.7) reports that Jesus' relatives kept their family records. Paul already calls Jesus "from the seed of David according to the flesh" (Romans 1:3) in the 50s. A betrothal before living together, a quiet divorce, and a father's naming of a son all fit Jewish custom of the time.
views.C: Most critical scholars think Matthew built the list from the Septuagint of Ruth and 1 Chronicles plus a source for the names after Zerubbabel, and that 1:18–25 is his own telling of an older tradition, shaped around Isaiah 7:14. Its differences from Luke show that neither copied the other here.
views.L: The chapter opens the frame of the whole Gospel: "God is with us" (1:23) answers to Jesus' last words (28:20). Matthew's first fulfillment formula (1:22) sets the pattern for the book, and Joseph, the obedient dreamer who does exactly what he is told (1:24), is the first model disciple.
views.J: The list reads like a Jewish family record, and its three eras follow Israel's story as Jews told it: promise, kingdom, exile, and waiting for restoration. Jewish readers have always pointed out that Isaiah 7:14 says "young woman" and spoke to King Ahaz, and that a son of David is reckoned through his father, which the story itself says Joseph was not. Later Jewish polemic (the Toledot Yeshu) answered the birth story with a rumor of illegitimacy.
views.T: The church fathers read the genealogy as the proof that the Son of God took real flesh from Israel and David. Ignatius of Antioch (about AD 110) already joins "of the family of David" and "from Mary" in his summary of the faith. The virgin birth entered the Apostles' Creed ("conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary") and the Nicene Creed. In the Western church, 1:18–25 is read in the last week of Advent; the Orthodox read the whole genealogy on the Sunday before Christmas.

deep.b:
Matthew runs forward from Abraham, Luke backward from Jesus to Adam (Luke 3:23–38). From Abraham to David the lists agree, because both follow Ruth 4 and 1 Chronicles 2. From David on they part: Matthew goes through Solomon and the kings of Judah, Luke through David's son Nathan and a line of unknown men. They meet briefly at Shealtiel and Zerubbabel, then part again, and they name different fathers for Joseph (Jacob in Matthew, Heli in Luke).

The main explanations are given in the note on 1:16. What both writers agree on matters as much as where they differ: Jesus was of David's line through Joseph, and Joseph was not his natural father. Luke makes this explicit: "People supposed he was Joseph's son" (Luke 3:23); Matthew shows it by breaking his own pattern in 1:16.

In about 734 BC the kings of Aram and Israel marched on Jerusalem to force King Ahaz into their alliance. Isaiah offered Ahaz a sign: a young woman, already pregnant or about to be, would have a son and name him Immanuel, and before the boy knew right from wrong, the two invading kings would be gone (Isaiah 7:14–16). Read in that setting, the child was born in Ahaz's time. Jewish interpreters have read it this way from antiquity, and many Christian scholars agree that this was its first meaning.

Christian readers have answered in three main ways. Some hold that the verse is a direct prediction of Jesus, since Isaiah 9:6–7 and 11:1–5 go on to describe a royal child far greater than any son of Ahaz. Some speak of a double fulfillment: a sign in Ahaz's day and a fuller one in Jesus. Others think Matthew, like other Jewish readers of his time, read the Greek text as a pattern now filled with new meaning. All agree that Matthew read the Septuagint's parthenos, and that his main interest is the name: God is with us.

echoes: Genesis 5:1; Genesis 38; Joshua 2; Ruth 4:13–22; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; 2 Samuel 11; 1 Chronicles 1:34; 1 Chronicles 2:1–15; 1 Chronicles 3:5–19; Isaiah 7:14; Isaiah 8:8–10; Psalm 130:8; Luke 1:26–38; Luke 2:1–7; Luke 3:23–38; 28:20

settings.to: The Gospel's readers, Jewish believers and their Gentile fellow believers, who knew Israel's story and its family lists
settings.when: The opening of the Gospel
settings.why: To show at the very start who Jesus is: the heir of the promises to Abraham and to David, and the goal of Israel's history, which the list divides into the rise to David, the fall to the exile, and the waiting for the Messiah. The four women prepare readers both for Gentiles in God's plan and for Mary's unexpected motherhood.
settings.readers: For a community arguing with other Jews over whether Jesus was the Messiah, a royal pedigree through Joseph answered the objection that he was a nobody from Galilee, and the women's names hinted that Gentile believers belonged in Abraham's family.

settings.by: An angel of the Lord, in a dream
settings.to: Joseph, a descendant of David, legally married to Mary but not yet living with her, who has just decided to divorce her quietly. Matthew names no town; he seems to place the family in Bethlehem (2:1, 2:11), unlike Luke, who has them come from Nazareth.
settings.when: While Joseph is still turning the matter over, after Mary is found to be pregnant
settings.why: To stop a righteous man from doing the righteous-looking thing. The angel tells Joseph that the child is from the Holy Spirit, that he must not be afraid to take Mary home, and that he is to name the boy, which will make Jesus his legal son and David's heir. It also tells him who the child will be: the one who saves his people from their sins.
settings.readers: For Matthew's readers, Jewish believers who may already have faced the charge that Jesus' birth was shameful (it is first recorded around AD 175, by Celsus), the scene answers: Joseph, a righteous son of David, knew everything and took Mary and the child as his own at God's command.

settings.to: The readers of the Gospel, Jewish believers in Jesus and their Gentile fellow believers, who knew the Scriptures and argued about them with other Jews
settings.when: Stepping out of the story after the angel's words
settings.why: To tell the reader how to see what has just happened: not as a scandal or an accident, but as God doing what he said through the prophet. It gives the name the angel did not give, Immanuel, and translates it, so that Greek-speaking readers grasp the claim: in this child, God is with us.
views: Many traditional readers hold that Isaiah directly foretold Jesus' birth from a virgin.
Many scholars think Matthew saw a sign given to Ahaz filled out more fully in Jesus, as he does with Hosea 11:1 in 2:15.

traditions.q: Did Mary remain a virgin after Jesus was born (1:25)?
views: Yes. Mary is "ever virgin": a virgin in conceiving Jesus, in giving birth and for the rest of her life. "Until" says nothing about after, and the "brothers" of Jesus are close relatives (Catechism 499–501, 510).
Yes. The church calls her Aeiparthenos, "Ever-Virgin," in its liturgy and councils (the Fifth Ecumenical Council, 553). The brothers of Jesus were Joseph's sons from an earlier marriage.

Luther held that Mary remained a virgin, and the Smalcald Articles (I.4, Latin text) call her "ever virgin." Lutherans today are divided: many treat it as a pious opinion, not a binding teaching, and many think she had other children.

Divided. Zwingli and Bullinger affirmed it, and the Second Helvetic Confession (chapter 11) calls Mary "ever virgin." Calvin would not argue either way from "until" or "firstborn," calling the question idle curiosity. The Westminster Standards say only "virgin," and most Reformed Christians today believe Mary and Joseph had children after Jesus.

No binding teaching: the Prayer Book and the Thirty-Nine Articles say only that Christ was born of the Virgin Mary. Many Anglican divines, such as Lancelot Andrewes and Jeremy Taylor, affirmed her perpetual virginity, and Anglo-Catholics still do; many evangelical Anglicans do not.

John Wesley believed Mary "continued a pure and unspotted virgin" after the birth (Letter to a Roman Catholic, 1749). Methodist doctrinal standards do not address it, and most Methodists today take the brothers as Mary's sons.
No. Mary was a virgin when Jesus was born, which Baptists firmly confess, but "until" and the brothers and sisters of 13:55–56 show that she and Joseph then had a normal marriage and other children.

title: The King the Nations Seek
sum: Magi from the east arrive in Jerusalem asking for the newborn king of the Jews, whose star they have seen. King Herod is alarmed. His chief priests and scribes find the answer in Micah: the Messiah will come from Bethlehem. Herod sends the magi there, pretending he wants to honor the child too. The star leads them to the house, and they bow down and give their gifts, then go home another way.

Warned in a dream, Joseph takes the child and Mary to Egypt. Herod has the boys of Bethlehem killed, and Matthew hears Rachel weeping. After Herod dies, Joseph brings the family back, but avoids Judea under Archelaus and settles in Nazareth in Galilee. At each step Matthew quotes Scripture: Jesus' early life retraces the story of Moses and of Israel, from Egypt to the promised land.
readings: The chapter fits what is known of Herod's last years: his fear of rivals, his killing of family members, the division of his kingdom and Archelaus's harsh rule. Star-watchers from Babylon or Persia could well have traveled to Judea, and Jewish hopes for a coming king were widely known in the east. The killing of a few boys in a small village would hardly reach Josephus's pages.
Read as a story built on Scripture

Many scholars think the chapter was shaped from Jewish stories of Moses' birth and from texts such as Numbers 24:17 (the star), Psalm 72 and Isaiah 60 (nations bringing gold and incense). In this reading Matthew's aim is not to report a sequence of events but to show who Jesus is: the king of Israel, recognized by the nations, opposed by the powerful, and the new Moses who relives Israel's exodus.

views.H: Herod died in 4 BC, so the story points to a birth around 6–4 BC. Archelaus ruled Judea 4 BC–AD 6 and was notorious for violence; Galilee under Antipas was quieter. There is no outside record of the magi or the killing of the children. Astronomers have proposed a conjunction in 7 BC, a comet in 5 BC, or an astrological event in 6 BC, but none can be shown to be Matthew's star.
views.C: This chapter is found only in Matthew, and Luke's birth story cannot easily be fitted with it (Luke has the family return from Bethlehem to Nazareth after forty days). Many critical scholars think Matthew drew on a story modeled on the infancy of Moses, organized around his fulfillment quotations (2:6; 2:15; 2:18; 2:23).
views.L: Each scene ends with a quotation, and each quotation names a place: Bethlehem, Egypt, Ramah, Nazareth. The chapter answers "where?" as chapter 1 answers "who?" Two kings stand side by side: Herod, who seeks the child to destroy him, and the child, whom the nations seek to honor. Joseph obeys three more dreams without a word.
views.J: Jewish readers would hear the Moses tradition: in Josephus and later Jewish retellings, Pharaoh is warned by his scribes of a coming deliverer. The chapter's harsh picture of Jerusalem's leaders belongs to Matthew's debate with other Jews; the people of Jerusalem in 2:3 are troubled, not hostile. Jeremiah 31:15 is still read in synagogues on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, and Rachel's tomb outside Bethlehem remains a place of Jewish prayer.
views.T: The magi became the first Gentiles to worship Christ, the "firstfruits of the nations." The Western church keeps them at Epiphany (January 6); the Eastern church keeps Epiphany as Jesus' baptism and joins the magi to Christmas. Irenaeus read the gifts as for a king, for God and for one who would die. The killed boys are honored as the Holy Innocents, the first martyrs for Christ.

deep.b:
Matthew and Luke agree on the central points: Jesus was born in Bethlehem, in Herod's time, to Mary, who was engaged to Joseph of David's line; he was conceived by the Holy Spirit; the angel gave the name Jesus; the family settled in Nazareth. But the episodes are different. Luke has the census, the manger, the shepherds, the Temple visit and the return to Nazareth; Matthew has the magi, the star, the flight to Egypt and the killing of the children. Matthew seems to assume the family lived in Bethlehem; Luke says they lived in Nazareth.

Harmonizers suggest that after the birth the family stayed on in Bethlehem for up to two years, received the magi there, fled to Egypt, and then went back to Nazareth (Luke 2:39 passing over the interval). Many critical scholars think the two stories cannot be fully fitted together and that each writer shaped the traditions he received to make his own point. Either way, the two accounts are independent of each other, which makes their shared core older than both.

echoes: Numbers 24:17; Micah 5:2; 2 Samuel 5:2; Psalm 72:10–15; Isaiah 60:1–6; Hosea 11:1; Jeremiah 31:15–17; Exodus 1:22; Exodus 2:15; Exodus 4:19–22; Isaiah 11:1; Judges 13:5; Luke 2:1–39; John 7:42

settings.to: People in Jerusalem, and through them King Herod
settings.when: On arrival in the capital, the obvious place to look for a royal birth
settings.why: Simply to find the newborn king and honor him. Without knowing it, they announce a rival king in Herod's own city, which sets the whole chapter in motion.
settings.readers: For Matthew's readers, in a church that was beginning to include Gentiles, the first people to honor Jesus in this Gospel are foreigners guided by a star, while Jerusalem's rulers are alarmed. The ending of the Gospel, with its mission to all nations (28:19), is already in view.

settings.what: The scholars' answer: Micah 5:2 with 2 Samuel 5:2
settings.by: The chief priests and scribes of the people
settings.to: King Herod, who has called them together
settings.when: Herod's inquiry after hearing the magi
settings.why: To answer the king's question correctly from Scripture: the Messiah will come from Bethlehem, David's town, and will shepherd God's people. The irony is that they serve Herod's plot with a text that promises a shepherd-king very unlike him.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, arguing with other Jews about whether Jesus was the Messiah, would note that the authorities themselves read Micah of Bethlehem, and that the evidence pointed to Jesus' birthplace (compare John 7:42).

settings.to: The magi, in a private meeting
settings.when: After he has learned when the star appeared and where the Messiah would be born
settings.why: To use the visitors as spies. His pious words ("so that I can come and bow down to him too") hide a plan to kill the child, as 2:16 shows.

settings.what: The angel's warning: flee to Egypt
settings.by: An angel of the Lord, in a dream
settings.to: Joseph, in Bethlehem
settings.when: Right after the magi leave
settings.why: To save the child's life. The order is precise and urgent, and Joseph carries it out that same night, as he did in 1:24.

settings.to: The Gospel's readers
settings.when: At the family's stay in Egypt, looking ahead to the return
settings.why: To show that Jesus, God's Son, relives the story of Israel, God's son, called out of Egypt. The quotation prepares for the voice at the baptism, "This is my Son" (3:17).
views: Most scholars, ancient and modern, read Hosea's verse as about Israel, which Matthew applies to Jesus as the one who sums up Israel.
Some traditional readers hold that Hosea's words also looked forward directly to the Messiah.

settings.to: The Gospel's readers
settings.when: After the killing of the boys of Bethlehem
settings.why: To give the grief of Bethlehem's mothers a voice from Scripture: Rachel weeping for her children in the exile. Readers who knew Jeremiah would remember that the next verses promise the children's return and a new covenant.

settings.what: The angel's word: return to Israel
settings.by: An angel of the Lord, in a dream
settings.to: Joseph, in Egypt
settings.when: After Herod's death
settings.why: To send the family back to the land. The words echo God's word to Moses in Midian (Exodus 4:19): the danger is past, and the deliverer can go back to his people.

settings.what: Fulfillment saying: "He will be called a Nazarene"
settings.to: The Gospel's readers, who knew Jesus as "the Nazarene" and may themselves have been called Nazarenes by others (compare Acts 24:5)
settings.when: At the family's settling in Nazareth
settings.why: To answer an objection: how could the Messiah come from an unknown village in Galilee? Matthew answers that even this fits "the prophets," probably by a wordplay on netser, the Branch of Isaiah 11:1.

title: A Voice in the Wilderness
sum: Years later John the Baptist appears in the Judean wilderness, calling Israel to repent because the kingdom of heaven has drawn near. Dressed like Elijah and living on desert food, he is the voice of Isaiah 40 preparing the Lord's road. Crowds come from Jerusalem and all Judea to confess their sins and be baptized in the Jordan. When Pharisees and Sadducees come, John warns them that being Abraham's children will not save them: the ax is at the root, and one stronger than John is coming to baptize in the Holy Spirit and fire.

Then Jesus comes from Galilee to be baptized. John protests, but Jesus says they must "fulfill all righteousness." As he comes up from the water, the heavens open, the Spirit comes down on him like a dove, and a voice from heaven declares, "This is my dearly loved Son." The hidden child of chapters 1–2 is now publicly named by God.
readings: John was a real prophet whose baptizing movement Josephus also describes, and Jesus' baptism by him is one of the best-attested facts about Jesus. The vision and the voice are reported as an experience of Jesus (in Mark, only he sees and hears), which historians cannot test, but they mark the start of his public work.

Israel passed through the waters of the Sea and the Jordan and was called God's son; then it was tested in the wilderness. Matthew tells Jesus' story in the same order: through the water (3:16), named as Son (3:17), led into the wilderness (4:1). Jesus stands where Israel stood, and does what Israel was called to do.

views.H: John's movement was large and lasting: Acts 19:1–7 finds disciples of John in Ephesus decades later. Josephus says Antipas feared John's influence. John's baptism, his call to repentance and his warning of coming judgment fit other Jewish renewal movements of the time, including the community at Qumran, but his once-for-all baptism by his own hand was new.
views.C: Matthew follows Mark 1:2–11 but adds John's preaching of judgment (3:7–10, 12), which he shares almost word for word with Luke 3:7–9, 17: the classic evidence for the sayings source Q, or for Luke's use of Matthew. Matthew alone adds John's protest and Jesus' reply (3:14–15), and changes the voice to "This is."
views.L: Jesus speaks for the first time in 3:15, and his first word is about fulfilling righteousness, a theme of the whole Gospel. John and Jesus preach the same opening message (3:2; 4:17), so John is presented as Jesus' forerunner and partner, not his rival. The Father's voice (3:17) answers the question chapters 1–2 raised: Jesus is God's Son.
views.J: John belongs fully within Judaism: a prophet in the line of Elijah, calling Israel back to God before the day of judgment, using purity washings that Jews knew well. His warning against trusting in descent from Abraham is a prophet's warning within the family, like Amos 9:7 or Jeremiah 7:4. The picture of the Pharisees and Sadducees as one group reflects Matthew's later debates more than the situation of John's time.
views.T: The Eastern churches celebrate Jesus' baptism on January 6 as Theophany, "God's appearing," when the Trinity was revealed: the Father's voice, the Son in the river, the Spirit as a dove. They bless the waters on that day. The fathers taught that Christ was baptized not to be cleansed but to cleanse the waters for Christian baptism (Ignatius; Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 39). John is honored as the Forerunner, the last of the prophets.

deep.b:
John's baptism was "for repentance" (3:11), and Christians believed Jesus was without sin (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22). So why did he come to be baptized? Matthew alone raises the question through John's protest (3:14). Jesus' answer, "to fulfill all righteousness," has been explained as obedience to God's will through his prophet, as Jesus standing with sinful Israel to carry their sins, or as the first step in fulfilling God's plan. The church fathers added that he was baptized to make water holy for all who would be baptized after him, and to show the Trinity.

Historians note the same tension from another side: the earliest followers of Jesus would hardly have invented a story that seemed to make him John's disciple or a sinner. Its presence in all the Gospels, with signs of discomfort in each, is a strong argument that it happened.

echoes: Isaiah 40:3; Malachi 3:1; Malachi 4:5–6; 2 Kings 1:8; Isaiah 51:1–2; Isaiah 11:2; Isaiah 42:1; Psalm 2:7; Genesis 22:2; Mark 1:2–11; Luke 3:1–22; John 1:19–34; Acts 19:1–7

settings.to: The crowds from Jerusalem, all Judea and the Jordan valley who came out to the wilderness
settings.when: The start of John's public preaching, around AD 28 (Luke 3:1 dates it to the fifteenth year of Tiberius)
settings.why: To get Israel ready for God's coming rule by calling every person to turn back to God, confess their sins and be baptized. In the wilderness setting the message meant that a new exodus was beginning and God's people were being formed again.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers would notice that John's message is word for word the message of Jesus (4:17) and, in part, of the disciples (10:7): one call runs from the forerunner to the church.

settings.to: The Gospel's readers
settings.when: Introducing John
settings.why: To identify John as the voice Isaiah promised, preparing a road for the Lord's return. By using "the Lord" for the one whose way John prepares, Matthew claims that in Jesus Israel's God is coming back to his people.

settings.what: John's warning to the Pharisees and Sadducees
settings.to: Many Pharisees and Sadducees who came to his baptism (in Luke 3:7, the crowds in general)
settings.when: As they arrive at the river
settings.why: To strip away false security. Coming to the river out of fear is not enough, and descent from Abraham does not protect anyone from judgment. Only a changed life counts, because the judge is about to arrive with his winnowing fork. John points beyond himself to the stronger one who will baptize in the Spirit and fire.
settings.readers: For Matthew's community, in conflict with the heirs of the Pharisees after AD 70, the scene shows that the leaders' opposition began with John, and that the line between God's people and others is drawn by fruit, not by birth.
views: Matthew aims the warning at the religious leaders, as he aims Jesus' later woes (chapter 23).
Luke gives the same words to the crowds and adds practical advice for tax collectors and soldiers (Luke 3:10–14). Many scholars think the source (Q) had a general audience and Matthew sharpened it.

settings.what: John and Jesus at the river
settings.to: Each other, at the Jordan
settings.when: As Jesus comes forward to be baptized
settings.why: John's protest says what he knows: Jesus is greater and needs no cleansing. Jesus' reply, his first words in Matthew, asks John to go ahead because it is God's will and part of God's righteous plan. It shows the reader that Jesus is baptized by choice, not from need.

settings.by: God the Father, speaking from heaven
settings.to: In Matthew, those present ("This is"); in Mark and Luke, Jesus himself ("You are")
settings.when: As Jesus comes up from the water and the Spirit descends
settings.why: To declare who Jesus is at the start of his work: the Son and king of Psalm 2, the beloved son like Isaac, and the servant of Isaiah 42 on whom God's Spirit rests. In Matthew the voice is an announcement: the reader and the witnesses are told.

traditions.q: What does Jesus' baptism mean for Christian baptism, and was John's baptism the same as ours?
views: John's baptism was a rite of repentance that prepared for Christ but did not give grace as Christian baptism does; the Council of Trent condemned the view that the two have the same effect (Session 7, canons on baptism, 1). By his baptism Jesus made the waters holy and showed the pattern of Christian baptism (Catechism 535–537, 1223–1225).

The feast of Theophany (January 6) celebrates the baptism as the revelation of the Trinity. Christ, who had no sin, entered the Jordan to sanctify water and all creation; the Great Blessing of Waters repeats this each year. John's baptism was a preparation; Christian baptism, given with chrismation, is new birth.

Luther's baptismal prayer says that by the baptism of his Son in the Jordan God "sanctified and set apart" the Jordan and all water as a saving flood. Christian baptism is God's own act through water and the word, not merely a human sign.

Calvin taught that John's baptism and the apostles' baptism were the same sacrament, since both were baptisms of repentance and forgiveness pointing to Christ (Institutes 4.15.7–8). The sign seals God's promise; it does not save by itself.

Jesus' baptism is the model: a person who has chosen to follow God is immersed and comes "up from the water" (3:16). So baptism is for believers only, by immersion, as a public act of obedience that pictures death and new life (Baptist Faith and Message, art. VII).

title: The Son Tested, the Light Rising
sum: Led by the Spirit into the wilderness, Jesus fasts forty days and nights and is tested by the devil. Three times the tester tries to bend the meaning of "God's Son": make bread for yourself, force God to rescue you, take the world's kingdoms by bowing to me. Three times Jesus answers with Moses' words in Deuteronomy, passing the tests Israel failed in its forty years. The devil leaves, and angels care for him.

When John is handed over, Jesus withdraws to Galilee and makes Capernaum his home: Isaiah's light rises on Zebulun and Naphtali, "Galilee of the nations." He begins to preach John's message, "Repent, because the kingdom of heaven has drawn near," and calls four fishermen, Simon Peter, Andrew, James and John, who leave their nets, their boat and their father to follow him. He teaches, proclaims and heals all over Galilee, and crowds from every region gather, ready for the Sermon on the Mount.
readings: Many readers take the testing as a real experience of Jesus, told in pictures: a struggle over how to use his calling as God's Son, perhaps told by Jesus himself to his disciples. The high mountain from which one sees every kingdom suggests a vision. What matters is the choice he made: trust, not proof; obedience, not power.
Read as Israel's story and a new Moses

The scene follows Israel's path: through the water (3:16), named as God's son (3:17), forty days in the wilderness for Israel's forty years, the same tests over bread, testing God and idolatry, answered from Moses' last speeches. Where Israel failed, Jesus is faithful. Read this way, Jesus is the true Israel and the new Moses, ready to give his teaching on the mountain (5:1).

views.H: A Jewish prophet withdrawing to the desert to fast before his mission fits the time, and Jesus' ministry centered on Capernaum and the villages of Galilee under Herod Antipas, among fishermen, farmers and tax collectors. The call of the first four disciples, known in all the Gospels, reflects real family partnerships in the lake's fishing trade.
views.C: Mark 1:12–13 mentions the testing in two verses; Matthew and Luke (4:1–13) share a long dialogue, a classic example of the material often credited to Q. Luke puts the Temple test last, placing Jerusalem at the climax; Matthew ends on the mountain with "Go away, Satan," the order most think was original. Matthew adds the Isaiah quotation (4:14–16) to Mark's summary of Jesus' move to Galilee.
views.L: The chapter closes Matthew's prologue. Jesus' identity as Son (3:17) is tested (4:1–11), his place is fixed in Galilee of the nations (4:12–16), his message is announced (4:17), his first followers are called (4:18–22), and a summary of his work (4:23), repeated almost word for word in 9:35, frames the teaching and healing of chapters 5–9.
views.J: The tests are answered entirely from Torah, in the manner of a Jewish teacher, and Gerhardsson read the scene as a Jewish midrash on Deuteronomy 6–8 and the Shema. Jewish readers note that Jesus here acts as a faithful Israelite, quoting the Shema's chapter on loving God with all one's heart. Galilee's Jewish villages, their synagogues and their fishermen are the world of the early rabbis' Galilee too.
views.T: The forty days became the model for Lent in the Western and Eastern churches, and in the Western churches the testing is read on the first Sunday of Lent. The fathers saw Christ as the new Adam who resisted where Adam fell, and as an example for Christians facing temptation. Peter and Andrew, James and John are honored as apostles; Andrew is called the "First-Called" in the Orthodox Church (from John 1:40).

deep.h: Three tests, three temptations of every age
deep.b:
Readers have drawn many lessons from the three tests. The church fathers compared them to the temptations of Adam and Eve ("good to eat," "a delight to the eyes," "attractive for making a person wise," Genesis 3:6) and to the "desire of the flesh, desire of the eyes and pride in possessions" of 1 John 2:16. Gerhardsson linked them to the Shema's heart, soul and strength. In Dostoevsky's novel The Brothers Karamazov (1880), the Grand Inquisitor names them miracle, mystery and authority: the powers by which leaders control people, which Jesus refused.

Whatever the lesson, Matthew's own concern is clear from the setting. The voice has just said "This is my dearly loved Son" (3:17), and each test asks what that means. The Son will not use his power for himself, will not force God to prove his care, and will not take the world's kingdoms without the cross. At the end of the Gospel he receives all authority in heaven and on earth from God (28:18), after obedience to death.

echoes: Deuteronomy 6:4–16; Deuteronomy 8:2–5; Psalm 91:11–12; Exodus 17:1–7; Exodus 34:28; Deuteronomy 34:1–4; 1 Kings 19:5–8; 1 Kings 19:19–21; Isaiah 9:1–7; 2 Kings 15:29; Mark 1:12–20; Mark 1:39; Luke 4:1–15; Luke 5:1–11; Luke 6:17–19; John 1:35–42; Hebrews 4:15

settings.what: The three tests and Jesus' answers from Deuteronomy
settings.to: Each other, alone in the wilderness, on the Temple and on a high mountain
settings.when: At the end of a forty-day fast, right after the voice at the baptism called Jesus God's Son
settings.why: The devil's words aim to turn Jesus' sonship into a reason to act on his own: to satisfy his hunger, to make God prove his care, to win the world by worshiping someone other than God. Jesus' answers, all from Moses' words to Israel in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 6–8), show a Son who lives on God's word, trusts without testing, and worships God alone.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, tempted to give up under pressure, or to seek proof and power, are shown how Jesus held on: by Scripture rightly understood and by single-minded loyalty to God. They are also shown that he is the faithful Israel their own Scriptures had longed for.

settings.to: The Gospel's readers
settings.when: At Jesus' move to Capernaum
settings.why: To explain why the Messiah's work begins in Galilee, not Jerusalem: Isaiah had promised that the northern land first darkened by Assyria's conquest would be the first to see a great light. The phrase "Galilee of the nations" also hints at the Gentiles who will one day share that light.
settings.readers: For a community of Jews and Gentiles, the quotation gave Scripture's backing both to Jesus' Galilean origins, which critics mocked (John 7:41, 52), and to the inclusion of the nations.

settings.to: The people of Galilee, in their towns and synagogues
settings.when: After John was handed over, from Capernaum on
settings.why: To announce that God's long-promised reign was arriving, and to call everyone to turn their lives around in response. By taking up John's exact words, Jesus carries on the work of the arrested prophet.

settings.what: The call of the first disciples
settings.to: Simon Peter and Andrew, fishermen casting nets on the Sea of Galilee, and then James and John, mending nets in their father's boat
settings.when: Early in Jesus' Galilean ministry, as he walked by the lake
settings.why: To call them to leave their work and follow him as his disciples, and to give them a new task: gathering people for God's kingdom. The call is sudden and costly, and it comes from Jesus' own authority, as a prophet like Elijah called Elisha.
settings.readers: For Matthew's readers, the scene is the pattern of every disciple's call: Jesus takes the initiative, the response is immediate, and following him comes before work and family. The same four are among the eleven sent out to make disciples of all nations at the end (28:16–20).

traditions.q: Should Christians keep a yearly forty-day fast (Lent) in memory of Jesus' forty days (4:2)?
views: Yes. "By the solemn forty days of Lent the Church unites herself each year to the mystery of Jesus in the desert" (Catechism 540). Lent is a season of prayer, fasting and almsgiving; Ash Wednesday and Good Friday are days of required fasting and abstinence (Catechism 1438, 2043).

Yes. Great Lent, the longest and strictest fast of the year, prepares for Pascha (Easter). The traditional rule gives up meat, dairy, fish, wine and oil on most days, adjusted by a spiritual father to each person's health and circumstances.

Yes. The Book of Common Prayer keeps Lent from Ash Wednesday; its collect for the first Sunday in Lent recalls that Christ fasted forty days and forty nights, and asks for grace to use such self-denial.

Lent is kept as part of the church year, but as a good order freely used, not a law binding the conscience; the Augsburg Confession rejects required fasts as a way to earn grace while praising fasting as training (art. 26).

The Westminster Directory for Public Worship (1645) recognized no holy days but the Lord's Day, so Puritans and many Presbyterians did not keep Lent, holding that the church may not bind consciences with days Scripture does not command. Many Reformed churches today observe Lent freely.

Baptists have no required church year, and many never kept Lent, stressing that Scripture commands no such season. Fasting is a personal discipline (6:16–18). In recent decades some Baptist churches have begun to mark Lent voluntarily.
